title: The British Expedition to Tibet
intro: The British expedition to Tibet, also called the Younghusband expedition, was effectively a temporary invasion by British Indian armed forces under the Tibet Frontier Commission. Its purported mission was to establish diplomatic relations and resolve the dispute over the Tibet–Sikkim border, and it was intended to counter perceived Russian ambitions.
ending: The Commission forced the Tibetan regent and National Assembly to sign the Convention of Lhasa on 7 September 1904, and the mission left in late September. Tibetan casualties have been estimated at between 2,000 and 3,000 killed or fatally wounded, and the British lost 202 men killed in action.

legs.title: From Sikkim to the Tibetan plateau

stops.text: Younghusband arrived in the capital of the princely state of Sikkim to prepare his mission. John Claude White, the political officer there, was unhappy with his secondment to the force.
stops.quote: On 19 July 1903, Younghusband arrived at Gangtok, the capital city of the British Indian princely state of Sikkim, where John Claude White was political officer, to prepare for his mission.

stops.text: Curzon had asked China and Tibet for talks here. The Dalai Lama refused to attend, and from August 1903 Younghusband and his escort commander, Lieutenant Colonel Brander, tried to provoke the Tibetans into a confrontation.
stops.quote: From August 1903, Younghusband and his escort commander at Khampa Dzong, Lieutenant Colonel Herbert Brander, tried to provoke the Tibetans into a confrontation.

stops.text: When no Tibetan or Chinese officials met the British at Khampa Dzong, Younghusband advanced to Tuna with some 1,150 soldiers, porters and labourers. After months of waiting in vain for negotiators, the expedition was ordered to continue toward Lhasa.
stops.quote: When no Tibetan or Chinese officials met the British at Khampa Dzong, Younghusband advanced with some 1,150 soldiers, porters, labourers, and thousands of pack animals, to Tuna, 50 miles beyond the border.

stops.text: A Tibetan force of 3,000 with matchlock muskets blocked the road behind a rock wall. After scuffles, the British, Sikh and Gurkha troops fired from three sides with Maxim guns. The Tibetans left between 600 and 700 dead and 168 wounded; British casualties were 12 wounded.
stops.quote: A military confrontation on 31 March 1904 became known as the Massacre of Chumik Shenko.

stops.text: The force reached the town after fighting at Red Idol Gorge on 9 April, where the Tibetans left 200 dead. The garrison had already left and the gates were opened. Younghusband's staff made Changlo Manor the Mission headquarters.
stops.quote: Following this fight at the "Red Idol Gorge", as the British later called it, the British military pressed on to Gyantse, reaching it on 11 April.

stops.text: After a breach was made in the Tibetan walls, Gurkhas and Royal Fusiliers took the fortress after eleven hours. Soldiers then pillaged Palkor Chode, Dongtse and other monasteries, and some of the pillaging was officially approved, according to Major Beynon.
stops.quote: The eventual assault on 6 July did not happen as planned, as the Tibetan walls were stronger than expected.

stops.text: After marching east from Gyantse on 14 July, the force passed along the shores of Yamdok Tso. It reached the fortress of Nakartse, empty except for a party of delegates from Lhasa. Younghusband would negotiate only at Lhasa.
stops.quote: They passed along the shores of the Yamdok Tso, and reached the fortress of Nakartse, unoccupied except for a party of delegates from Lhasa.

stops.text: The force found that the 13th Dalai Lama had fled to Urga, the capital of Outer Mongolia. The Amban escorted the British into the city but said he had no authority to negotiate.
stops.quote: The force arrived in Lhasa on 3 August 1904 to discover that the thirteenth Dalai Lama had fled to Urga (now Ulaanbaatar), the capital of Outer Mongolia.

stops.text: Younghusband intimidated the regent, Ganden Tri Rinpoche, and the Tsongdu into signing the Convention of Lhasa, which he had drafted. It was signed at his insistence at the Potala. It set an indemnity of 7,500,000 rupees and put the Chumbi Valley under British occupation until it was paid.
stops.quote: Eventually however Younghusband intimidated the regent, Ganden Tri Rinpoche, and the Tsongdu (Tibetan National Assembly), into signing a treaty on 7 September 1904, drafted by himself, known subsequently as the Convention of Lhasa. It was signed, again at Younghusband's insistence, at the Potala Palace.

notes: The Jelep La is not in the article, so it is left out. Gnathong (army left 11 December 1903) left out because the article's order of Tuna and the December departure is unclear. Left out as no points or no dates: Kangma, Red Idol Gorge (a gorge), Naini, Tsechen, Chushul Chakzam and the Tsangpo crossing (25 July, a river crossing). Tuna and Nakartse have no date in the article, so date and year are null; 'Tuna, Tibet' may not be the exact Wikipedia title. Guru: the article's name for the massacre is Chumik Shenko. Gyantse stop text uses the article's 9 April Red Idol Gorge fight. The Gyantse Dzong text on pillaging is from the article's paragraph after the storming; the looting at Tsechen monastery on 28 June is not given a stop. Casualty figures are as the article gives them, without attribution beyond 'estimated'. Chinese and Tibetan interpretations (article's last section) are not in the stops.
